design_judgment.intended_result: The set states one coherent product result and one reader decision per layer: the Charter decides whether a capability is Runtime's, the portable T0 decides which identity survives provider and backend replacement, the T1 root decides which single owner holds a responsibility and in which direction it may depend, and each T2 answers one implementable question. The public host lifecycle still enumerates identically across Charter section 7 item 3, T0 section 6, T1 section 5.1, and Execution section 2 (start, bounded status and result refs, cancel, authorized external event, reconcile, recover), so the Charter completion gate cannot pass while a required public operation is absent. All twenty carried findings are genuinely closed against the revised bytes, not merely asserted closed. Revision 1: f01 common `RuntimeExecution` is now registered in T0 section 3.2 and T1 section 4 and used by 04/10; f02 T1 section 6 step 4 names per-origin start facts; f03 Invocation section 2 makes Workflow Execution conditional and section 12 item 13 exercises the module origin; f04 Source Architecture rule 6 and conformance item 12 resolve Invocation's authorization edge through a host-provided validator; f05 Registry section 3 registers the family and section 11 item 21 carries the evidence; f06 T1 section 9.3 and Inspection section 6 make the export a non-persistent governed derivative; f07 the partial Ingress frontmatter `inherits` key is gone; f08 Conformance sections 3, 4, and 9 item 10 are host-neutral; f09 the t2 manifest evidence matches the 21-item enumeration; f10 T1 section 3 now carries EXECUTION and INSPECTION foundation edges; f11 the PostgreSQL preference is gone from Invocation section 4; f12 Inspection section 4 and the reader gain cover both origins. Revision 2: f01 Execution section 2.1 now names a host-provided Product Authorization decision-validator protocol and section 11 item 17 makes it checkable; f02 Execution section 4 supplies the request-bound `InvocationHost`, orders the dynamic intent commit, and section 11 item 18 proves it, with matching text in Invocation section 6 and Ledger section 5.3; f03 Ledger sections 3 rule 1 and 5.1 commit and idempotently reuse the one root Module Run; f04 Registry sections 3 and 6 make `execution_variant_policy` a distinct family with its own activation scope and Execution section 3 binds that name; f05 the complete subject manifest now declares the portable governance source as canonical target, the project file as a mechanical projection, and the distribution owner's acceptance as an adoption blocker; f06 the four conformance enumerations each close once; f07 T1 section 2 says 'the Design Doc contract registry'; f08 Durability section 9 is now 'Backend Adapter Mapping' with no named-backend mechanics. What remains are three local defects, all on or adjacent to the protected-operation path that revision 3 rewrote.
design_judgment.authority_structure: Each of the six responsibilities keeps exactly one primary T2 owner in T1 section 2, and 02, 03, 05, and 09 remain explicitly specializing or validating. No seventh responsibility appears: the supporting foundation, physical directories, repository planes, and named backends are each labelled as a source class, plane, or replaceable binding. Duplicated authority is refused where it would most easily appear: Registry section 8 is its own enforcement point and disclaims document 09's ports; document 09 section 4 disclaims becoming a central PEP; Ledger section 6 owns durable fence comparison while 09 owns fence meaning and 10 owns finalization timing; Inspection section 1 reconciles its `get_execution` view against Execution's `get_status`; Registry validates Variant Policy schema and Profile admission while Execution alone validates coverage. Two authority-source residues remain, both local and both created by the revision-3 dynamic-operation rewrite. First, for one dynamic Invocation-owned protected operation the set now names two independent decision sources — Invocation's host-provided Product Authorization validator in 08 sections 5 and 6, and document 09's `authorize_protected_operation` observation in 09 section 5 — while Execution section 4 step 6 says Execution itself 'validates current decision or grant evidence', and no document says which observation the Ledger intent's required `authority-observation refs` binds or which decision governs when they differ. Second, `ExternalAuthorityInvalidationSink` is declared as an inbound boundary for pushed external invalidation, yet no responsibility publishes an enforcement point or `ResourcePermissionManifest` action for it and it is absent from the four-document public-lifecycle enumeration, unlike the Ingress port which explicitly refuses to be a second host entry surface.
design_judgment.boundary_coherence: Semantic owner, author, operator, reviewer, persistence owner, implementation binding, and approval authority stay distinct almost everywhere they meet. Registry and Ledger own record and schema meaning while Data Governance binds System of Record and writer boundary and Software Delivery admits migration code; Contract Audit owns the independent verdict while Design Doc Management owns admission of canonical text; document 05 assembles evidence and refuses to publish or deploy, and its section 10 routes the predecessor roadmap disposition to Design Doc Management and the Software Delivery owner rather than to a Code Design Basis; Source Architecture section 7 keeps logical ownership, physical placement, packaging, and generation authority labelled rather than presented as peers. The revision-3 portable-source declaration is coherent: the manifest names `09_soul/governance/t0/the_agent_runtime.md` as canonical target with the project file as mechanical projection, which matches the candidate's own section 12, Design Doc Management section 9's governance distribution owner, and section 5.1's rule that project additions do not silently mutate reusable law; the document's `canonical_owner: designDoc/the_agent_runtime.md` field follows the existing portable-package convention for the installed project surface and is not a second authority claim. The remaining boundary defect is the pushed-invalidation intake: it mutates canonical execution state across a service boundary with no named Policy Enforcement Point, no declared grant class, and no place in the public handoff list, even though T1 section 12 requires an 'invalidation' port as a machine contract.
design_judgment.inheritance_and_dependencies: Inherited constraints are named per document and close. The Timestamp Semantics registered predicate, immutable `DistributedClockProfile`, fresh per-domain `ClockHealthEvidence`, and section 8 conservative half-open window are consumed identically by Registry section 8, Ledger sections 3 and 6, document 09 sections 3 and 6, Inspection section 2, Ingress section 7, and Execution section 6, and every one fails closed; the Ledger store alone assigns `recorded_at_utc`, and Execution and Invocation both disclaim assigning it. Product Authorization's grant-class law, `ResourcePermissionManifest` obligation, and Principal-versus-workload-actor separation are consumed without redefinition, as is Data Governance's derivative-inheritance and export law. Dependency direction is acyclic and enforceable: Source Architecture section 3 places T2 03 and T2 09 source inside Execution, so cross-responsibility edges reduce to Execution to Registry, Invocation, Durability, and Ledger; Invocation to Registry; Inspection to Registry and Ledger; and everything to the foundation. `DurableDispatchSink` and `InvocationHost` are both correctly owned by the lower responsibility and implemented above it, so neither creates a reverse import or a second Ledger writer. Two residues remain. The T1 section 3 diagram, corrected in revision 2 for its missing foundation edges, still omits INGRESS to REGISTRY and INGRESS to LEDGER even though Ingress sections 2 and 4 declare both; document 02 covers this because ingress source is intra-Execution, so no enforcement conflict exists. And the Ledger transaction families give the protected-operation-intent batch no atomic claim-and-fence validation, unlike the claim and finalization batches, so the check-then-commit sequence that guards resource entry is not stated to serialize against a concurrent invalidation.
design_judgment.intent_code_separation: Stable intent is well separated from mutable truth. Every T2 ends with a change boundary that refuses to freeze fields, select a provider, or migrate data; the code architecture audit's current-code observations are consistently held as evidence inputs rather than design, and its explicit self-limitation to a non-frozen dirty worktree is respected. Durability section 9 no longer carries one backend's Signal, Update, query, retry, and Continue-As-New mechanics; it states only the provider-neutral obligation that a named backend's primitives must satisfy the command-identity, acknowledgement, `DurableReadyEvent`, and bounded-snapshot laws before an Adapter release is admitted, with exact mappings pushed into the code-owned Adapter Release. Invocation section 4 states only 'a host-provided enforcing data-access capability' with the concrete binding declared outside stable intent. Conformance section 3 gives the general no-host-coupling rule and pushes exact excluded package identities into the code-owned profile; Inspection section 13 records the concrete store binding only in the evidence record. The one wording residue is Execution section 3's 'Runtime-issued Execution Variant Policy release', which reads as Runtime authoring a release while Registry section 4 and T0 section 9 state that Runtime only admits externally submitted structured candidate bundles.
design_judgment.implementability: Most of the set is implementable without redesign. Start, dispatch, finalization, event application, cancellation, invalidation, acknowledgement, recovery, and reconciliation converge idempotently across every declared crash and race window without claiming cross-system atomicity or a second Ledger. Both origins are complete and symmetric: Ledger sections 3 and 5.1 commit and idempotently reuse one root Module Run for the Module origin, Execution section 4 refuses waits and external events for that origin, Ingress section 4 refuses a non-Workflow origin, Invocation section 12 item 13 exercises it, and Inspection section 4 renders both. Provider/model A/B Variants, Runtime retry, backend delivery retry, reviewer revision lineage, provider-context reconstruction, and new execution stay distinct across 01, 07, 08, and 10. Inspection filters authorized scope at storage before disclosure and keeps content permissions separate; Standalone Release Conformance freezes one exact subject including generated Design Contract bundle parity and stays out of Software Delivery and Contract Audit. `RuntimeCohesionSignalReport` remains the only object I would question on economy and is defensible as explicitly advisory. Two gaps would still force a Code Design Basis to invent semantics, both inside the newly written dynamic-operation path: which authorization observation the dynamic protected-operation intent binds and whether Execution independently decides or only verifies Invocation's evidence; and whether the intent commit atomically revalidates the active claim and current fence or trusts a prior non-atomic read, which is what decides whether Execution section 8's claim that invalidation 'prevents new dispatch and protected operations' is enforceable. Each is correctable inside an existing owner without adding a layer, port, or process.

findings.quoted_evidence: Ledger 04 section 5.3 requires the intent contents: "Before a model call, Gateway call, external effect, or other protected operation begins, Ledger commits the exact operation identity, parent Attempt, authority-observation refs, resource/action scope, and idempotency identity." Invocation 08 section 6 enumerates the dynamic intent without them: "The host verifies the active Attempt claim and current durable fence, commits an operation intent that binds Attempt lineage, action, resource, input hash, Timestamp-governed deadline and duration budget, and idempotency identity, and only then enters the admitted resource callable." Its decision source is Invocation's own: "For each dynamic tool call, Invocation validates its own `ResourcePermissionManifest` through the host-provided Product Authorization validator, then hands the exact request and decision evidence to `InvocationHost`." Document 09 section 5 states a different flow for the same operation class: "External Authority Integration returns one `ProtectedOperationAuthorityObservation` containing the exact decision, context, status, grant disposition when required, predicate, clock profile, health evidence, validity window, and enforcing audience refs and hashes. Ledger records the observation. The enforcing responsibility applies it before entering the resource." Execution 10 section 4 step 6 adds a third actor: "for each dynamic operation requested during Invocation, validates current decision or grant evidence, revalidates the active claim and durable fence, commits the exact intent, and only after its receipt permits the host bridge to enter the admitted resource;".
findings.requirement: T1 section 2 requires that "Each Runtime responsibility that owns a protected resource acts as the Policy Enforcement Point for its own operations under Product Authorization and publishes its own `ResourcePermissionManifest`" and assigns document 09 "protected-operation authority observations" while stating that it "does not become a central Runtime PEP and does not replace Registry or Invocation enforcement". Ledger 04 section 5.3 requires that "Observation after the operation cannot manufacture this prior authority", and document 09 conformance item 13 requires that "audit reconstruction joins external authority, Runtime Ledger, and resource-owner evidence without making a projection authoritative".
findings.impact: For one dynamic tool or Gateway call the set now names two independent decision sources and three actors, and does not say which observation the required `authority-observation refs` of the Ledger intent binds. A Code Design Basis must invent one of three incompatible answers: record only Invocation's host-validator decision evidence, in which case document 09's `authorize_protected_operation` never participates in the dynamic path it explicitly describes and the audit join in 09 item 13 has no external-authority ref to join on; record only a document-09 observation obtained by Execution, in which case the decision that actually admits the resource is not the one Invocation's enforcement point made; or record both, in which case no document states precedence when the two disagree and Execution becomes a second enforcement point for Invocation-owned resources, which T1 section 2 and document 09 section 4 forbid. Because the intent commit is what proves prior authority before an external effect, the ambiguity sits on the security-bearing path rather than a presentational one.
findings.accountable_owner_ref: Agent Runtime Execution T2 design owner of designDoc/agent_runtime_10_execution_contract.md, which T1 section 2 names as owner of "Public host lifecycle, Workflow and Module coordination, Attempt policy, Evaluation, Selection, Resolution, cancellation, and reconciliation" and which is the only responsibility legally holding both document 09's ports and the `InvocationHost` implementation
findings.required_change: In Execution section 4, state exactly which authorization observation the Execution-supplied `InvocationHost` binds into the dynamic protected-operation intent, whether document 09's `authorize_protected_operation` is invoked for dynamic Invocation-owned operations, and whether Execution's "validates current decision or grant evidence" is an independent decision or verification of the evidence Invocation supplies. Align Invocation section 6's enumeration of the dynamic intent contents and document 09 section 5's "enforcing responsibility applies it" sentence to that single answer, and extend Execution conformance item 18 so the recorded observation refs are machine-checkable.

findings.quoted_evidence: Ledger 04 section 5.3 places the guard outside the transaction: "For a dynamic operation discovered after Invocation begins, the Execution-supplied `InvocationHost` verifies the active Attempt claim and current durable fence, submits this exact intent through the Execution-owned Ledger writer, and waits for the commit receipt before entering the admitted resource callable." The two neighbouring families state the guard inside the transaction. Section 5.2: "One claim transaction checks the current dispatch state, existing Outcome, active Variant, next legal Attempt ordinal, retry eligibility supplied by Execution, and current authority fence." Section 5.4: "One finalization transaction: 1. verifies the active claim and parent lineage; 2. reads the current durable authority-fence facts...". Section 6 scopes the comparison to finalization only: "Ledger owns the durable fence facts and executes the exact registered comparison inside the same transaction that would make an Attempt result authoritative." Section 9's failure table has no row for an operation intent submitted under a stale claim or closed fence, while Execution 10 section 8 promises prevention: "Authority invalidation prevents new dispatch and protected operations and leads to `authorization_invalidated` when no newly authorized compensation branch exists."
findings.requirement: the_agent_runtime section 6 invariant 2 requires that "the durable intent and active fence are committed before the corresponding external effect". T1 section 7 step 4 requires that "Required protected-operation intents are committed before external access", and T1 section 7 assigns the transaction families: "Document 04 owns the record and transaction families". Ledger section 2 already claims the obligation for this record family: "Authority binding, protected-operation intent, invalidation, and fence value | External Authority Integration and Execution | Preserve exact refs and perform the registered atomic comparison".
findings.impact: Section 2 says this record family carries the registered atomic comparison, section 6 restricts that comparison to finalization, and section 5.3 gives the intent batch no validation at all, leaving the claim and fence check as a caller-side read before an unvalidated append. An implementer reading section 5.3 literally builds a non-validating insert, so an invalidation committed between the `InvocationHost` read and the intent commit still admits the intent and permits resource entry, and Execution section 8's "prevents new dispatch and protected operations" and Invocation section 6's "A denied call or failed intent commit never enters the resource implementation" become best-effort rather than enforceable. The choice also changes the batch schema and the failure vocabulary for the one Ledger family that guards external effects, so guessing wrong propagates into every dynamic tool and Gateway path.
findings.accountable_owner_ref: Agent Runtime Execution Ledger T2 design owner of designDoc/agent_runtime_04_execution_ledger_contract.md, which T1 section 2 names as owner of "Canonical execution facts, content refs, atomic batches, durable authority-fence facts, monotonic append order, atomic fence comparison, custody facts, query ports"
findings.required_change: State in section 5.3 whether the protected-operation intent transaction itself verifies the active Attempt claim and current durable fence fail closed, on the pattern already used by sections 5.2 and 5.4, or explicitly state that it does not and name where the resulting race is absorbed. Add the matching row to the section 9 failure table and the matching obligation to section 10, then confirm that Execution section 8 and Invocation section 6 describe the same guarantee.

findings.quoted_evidence: Document 09 section 2 declares an external inbound boundary: "`ExternalAuthorityInvalidationSink` is the provider-neutral inbound boundary for pushed invalidation. Every submission carries trusted external-authority request context, the exact execution authority binding ref and hash, the monotonic external status or fence value, and immutable evidence refs." Execution 10 section 2.1's manifest does not cover it: "resource types for Runtime execution origins, active executions, external event targets, cancellation targets, and reconciliation cases; atomic actions `start`, `get_status`, `request_cancellation`, `submit_external_event`, `reconcile`, and `recover`". T1 section 5.1's complete public lifecycle likewise lists only six operations, while T1 section 12 still requires an "operation-intent, invalidation, and reconciliation ports" machine contract. The sibling external intake states the opposite rule; Ingress 03 section 2: "`ExternalEventIngressPort` is an intra-Execution contract exported through the Execution namespace. It is not a second host entry surface. The trusted host calls only `RuntimeExecutionService.submit_external_event`; Execution invokes this port."
findings.requirement: T1 section 2 requires that "Each Runtime responsibility that owns a protected resource acts as the Policy Enforcement Point for its own operations under Product Authorization and publishes its own `ResourcePermissionManifest`", while document 09 section 4 disclaims that role: "This document does not become a central Runtime PEP and does not replace Registry or Invocation enforcement." Execution section 2.1 requires the bounded `OperationGrant` class for external calls that "mutate canonical execution state across a service boundary".
findings.impact: A pushed invalidation advances the monotonic fence, stops new dispatch and protected operations, and drives an execution toward `authorization_invalidated`, which is a canonical execution-state mutation arriving across a service boundary. Its intake is declared as a port but is absent from every public-lifecycle enumeration and from the only manifest that could authorize it, and its owner explicitly refuses to be an enforcement point, so no document says who authorizes the submission or under which grant class. The Charter section 7 item 3 completion gate can therefore pass on the six enumerated operations while the seventh inbound external boundary has no owner. The pull fallback in document 09 section 2 keeps the design workable and bounds the exposure to a denial-of-availability path rather than authority widening, which is why this is a local correction rather than a missing public boundary, but it must be assigned before a Code Design Basis exposes the sink.
findings.accountable_owner_ref: Agent Runtime External Authority Integration T2 design owner of designDoc/agent_runtime_09_external_authority_integration_contract.md, which T1 section 2 names as owner of "Execution-time external-authorization and governed-data observation ports, operation intents, fence-value semantics, invalidation, late-result quarantine, and newly authorized compensation requests"
findings.required_change: State in section 2 whether `ExternalAuthorityInvalidationSink` is an intra-Execution contract that a trusted host reaches only through a named `RuntimeExecutionService` action, following the rule Ingress 03 section 2 already applies, or a distinct external surface. If it is reachable from outside Runtime, name the enforcing responsibility and require that responsibility's `ResourcePermissionManifest` to declare its resource type, action, and grant requirement class, and cross-reference the resulting entry in Execution section 2.1 and the public handoff list in T1 section 5.1 so the enumerated lifecycle and the actual inbound surfaces match.

findings.quoted_evidence: T1 section 3 introduces the diagram with "The target logical dependency direction is:" and gives the ingress node only two outbound edges: "INGRESS --> FOUNDATION" and "INGRESS --> AUTHORITY", plus the inbound "EXECUTION --> INGRESS". Ingress 03 section 2 declares two more: "The port consumes Registry and Ledger query contracts plus document 09's external-authority port." Section 4 repeats the Ledger dependency: "Ingress reads the exact current Ledger state and pinned Workflow Release."
findings.requirement: T1 section 3 presents the graph as normative target direction while delegating exactness: "Document 02 owns the exact machine-checked allowed-import graph, public-surface manifest, file ownership, and migration-debt high-water mark." This is the same class corrected in revision 2 as finding f10, where the two missing foundation edges were added rather than the diagram relabelled.
findings.impact: Read literally, the root forbids Ingress from consuming the Registry and Ledger query contracts that its own T2 requires in two sections. No enforcement conflict arises because Source Architecture section 3 places ingress source inside Execution, which already holds both edges, but the root diagram is again a non-subset of the enforced graph and invites an implementer to encode the wrong edge set for the supporting node class.
findings.accountable_owner_ref: Agent Runtime T1 design owner of designDoc/agent_runtime_00_runtime_domain_contract.md
findings.required_change: Add INGRESS --> REGISTRY and INGRESS --> LEDGER so the root diagram remains a correct subset of document 02's graph, or label the root diagram explicitly as illustrative class-level direction whose exact edge set is owned by document 02.

findings.quoted_evidence: Execution 10 section 3: "One start command binds exact host execution binding, origin release, input package, Runtime-issued Execution Variant Policy release, external authority context, governed-input scope, durable Adapter binding, and stable idempotency identity." The same section repeats it: "The host forwards this Runtime release and cannot add or replace a Profile." Registry 01 section 4 states the only authoring path: "An external authoring adapter reads that source and submits one structured `RuntimeReleaseCandidateBundle` containing canonical candidate bytes and declared relationships." Registry section 6 admits the policy on the same terms: "An Execution Variant Policy is admitted independently from a Workflow, Module, or Behavior Policy and is referenced by exact release identity from the host execution binding."
findings.requirement: the_agent_runtime section 9 states that "Runtime only admits a structured immutable candidate bundle through Registry", and Registry section 1 states that Registry "turns one structured, content-addressed candidate submission into individually identified immutable releases" and that it "does not decide ... which model or provider should execute a Module".
findings.impact: An Execution Variant Policy is mandatory in every start and determines which admitted Execution Profile, and therefore which provider and model, runs every node. Calling it 'Runtime-issued' reads as Runtime authoring the release, which no responsibility owns and which contradicts the admit-only boundary stated by the T0 and Registry. The words 'admitted Registry Execution Variant Policy Release' two sentences later give the correct meaning, so no authority actually moves, but a Code Design Basis could build a Runtime-side policy issuer that Registry section 4 does not admit.
findings.accountable_owner_ref: Agent Runtime Execution T2 design owner of designDoc/agent_runtime_10_execution_contract.md
findings.required_change: Replace 'Runtime-issued' with wording that names the release class rather than an issuer, for example 'admitted Runtime Execution Variant Policy release', so section 3 cannot be read as giving Runtime authority to author a release that Registry admits from an external structured candidate bundle.

safe_next_step: Return the complete candidate to the Runtime design owner for a revision 4 that applies three corrections inside their existing owners plus two notes; do not freeze a Code Design Basis, replace canonical Design Docs, or begin source restructuring on this revision. Apply f01 first in Execution section 4, because the dynamic protected-operation decision source and the observation refs it binds are what Invocation section 6, document 09 section 5, and Ledger section 5.3 must all restate consistently; then f02 in Ledger sections 5.3, 9, and 10, so the intent batch's claim-and-fence validation is fixed before any batch schema work and Execution section 8's invalidation claim becomes enforceable; then f03 in document 09 section 2, naming the enforcement point and reachable surface for pushed invalidation and cross-referencing Execution section 2.1 and T1 section 5.1 so the enumerated public lifecycle and the actual inbound surfaces agree. Apply the two notes in the same pass (f04 in T1 section 3, f05 in Execution section 3). Then re-freeze one whole-system candidate with updated hashes and carried predecessor findings and submit revision 4 for independent whole-system semantic review. The declared missing formal Runtime review host, the portable-source acceptance by the governance distribution owner, the canonical filename-owner collisions, the predecessor lifecycle dispositions, and the unfrozen Code Design Basis remain open and correctly disclosed; none is closed by this review, and this result stays advisory until the formal Design Contract reviewer binding exists.
